WRITTEN ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS 
Disappearance of listed BSE companies 
*21.     SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: 
SHRI JIBON ROY: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that at least 2750 companies of 
the 5651 listed on the BSE were not available for trading and have gone 
missing with around Rs. 10,000 crore invested in these companies by 
millions of investors; 
(b) if so, how many of them have been officially declared as 
'disappeared' and the total amount of investors' money involved therein; 
and 
(c) what steps are being taken to ensure that the listed companies 
do not play 'Loot and Scoot' game with investors' money? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (c) 
No, Sir. However, the Central Coordination and Monitoring Committee of 
Securities and Exchange Board of India and the Department of Company 
Affairs has informed that of the 7050 issues during the period 1992-98, 185 
companies could be identified as 'vanishing companies'. In these companies, 
the total monetary exposure involved is approximately Rs. 1150 crores. Of 
these companies, the total monetary exposure involved is approximately Rs. 
1150 crores. Of these 185 companies, 82 with total issue size (amount 
involved) of approximately Rs. 600 crores responded to the notices issued by 
SEBI and have, therefore, been cl assified as 'resurfaced vanishing 
companies'. The Department of Company Affairs has taken action including 
filing

Action on Tarapore Committee Report 
*23.     SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: 
SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMAD KHAN (DURRU): 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken any follow-up action with regard to the 
officials indicted by the Tarapore Comm ittee in January, 2002 In the U.T.I, 
scam; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) by when action is likely to be taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (c) 
After detailed audit, and as recommended by the Tarapore Committee, 19 
cases were referred to the Advisory Board for Banking, Commercial and 
Financial Frauds (ABBCFF); which is a pre-investigative body under the 
Central Vigilance Commission. As the transactions/investment 
4 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
decisions commented upon by the Tarapo re Committee are essentially capital 
market related transactions, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) 
is the regulator in this regard. Therefore, the Government, in consultation with 
SEBI have referred 89 cases for inquiry by them (SEBI). 
In addition based on the recommendation of the Tarapore Committee, a 
departmental enquiry against officials of UTI was conducted, consequentially 
a former ED indicted, against whom a complaint was then lodged with the 
CBl.Two additional cases, inquired intern ally by the UTI, have also been 
lodged with the CBI.

Statement-I 
Relevant Extracts from the minutes of the meeting of the appointments boards 
held in RBI, New Delhi on 11th October, 2000 
Agenda Item No. 2 
Procedure for appointment of whole time Directors in Public Sector 
Banks 
The Appointments Boar d recognized the need  for providing for a 
reasonable tenure for Whole Time Direct ors in Public Sector Banks in order 
to ensure that the bank gets the benefit of continuity in leadership in an era of 
increasing competition along with a fair method of selection based on merit 
with due consideration to seniority, for maintaining the morale and 
motivation of employees. The issue of re sidual service for Chief Executive in 
an institution matters a lot, as a Chief Executive with very short tenure implies 
lack of long-term commitment and vision and gaps in formulation and 
implementation of the long-term policy for the organisation. It was also felt 
that the whole issue of Co rporation Governance, which inter alia prescribes 
autonomy with accountability of the top management necessarily demands a 
minimum reasonable tenure for Chief Executives, which will avoid 
uncertainty and ensure continuity of policy. 
The Appointments Board also noted that the introduction of a procedure 
prescribing minimum tenure for appointment of whole time director will give 
rise to super-session of a few persons with excellent 
8 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
record for the top position on ground of their residual service being less than 
the minimum prescribed. However, the situation of super-session of otherwise 
qualified and competent persons will emerge at any time, when a transition 
from merit-cum-seniority procedure to tenure-oriented procedure is made. It 
was recognized that this may create resentment among some persons and may 
impinge on building organisational teams at higher levels. 
The Appointments Boar d also recognized th at the procedure for 
prescribing minimum tenure for whole time directors in State Bank of India 
(SBI) keeping in view its special stat us, large size and trained and skilled 
manpower, may be somewhat different from the one which may be followed 
for the nationalised banks. Keeping in view the constraints of public sector 
character of these banks and the existing guidelines of Department of 
Personnel and Training, the Appointments Board suggested that the following 
system may be followed by the Board while considering candidates for 
appointment as whole-time directors on the Boards of public sector banks:— 
(a) For Chairman and Managing Direct or of SBI—a minimum residual 
service of two years from the date the vacancy arises. 
(b) For Managing Director of SBI—a minimum residual service of one 
year from the date the vacancy arises. 
(c) For Chairman and Managing Director of Nationalised Banks— All 
persons with minimum residual service of two years as on 1st April of 
the financial year in which vacancy arises will be considered. 
However, it should be kept in view that the person who is 
recommended for a particular nationalised bank should as far as 
feasible, have at least two years of service in the concerned bank. 
(d) For executive Directors of Nationalised Banks—A minimum residual 
service of two years as on 1st April ot the concerned financial year 
shall be considered for the purpose of calling people for interview…"

Technology for rain water 
*26. SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the technology of using rain water has 
declined in the country; 
(b) if so, the steps Government propose to take for the optimum use of rain 
water; 
10 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(c) whether it is also a fact that Stat e Governments are not in a position 
to exploit the rivers and ground water in a better way; and 
(d) if so, what steps, Government propose to take for the full utilisation 
of river water? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) and (b) No, Sir. The technology of using rain water either 
directly through rain water harvesting or by way of development of surface 
water and ground water resources ha s not declined in the country. The 
technology has relatively improved ov er the time. The modern techniques 
and technology are being used in water resources planning, development and 
management with a view to optimise the utilisation of water resources. 
(c) State Governments, in general, are properly equipped for using latest 
technology for development of water resources. However, for optimum 
utilisation of water resources, both surface water and ground water, it is 
necessary to adopt the comprehensive and integrated approach for water 
resources planning, development and management. 
(d) In order to achieve full development of utilisable water resources, 
additional live storage capacity of 75 BCM will be created on completion of 
a number of dams under various stages of construction. Government of India 
is providing central loan assistance under Accelerated Irrigation Benefits 
Programme (AIBP) since 1996-97 to he lp the State Governments in their 
efforts to harness rain water and acceler ate creation of irrigation potential by 
speedy completion of certain selected ongoing schemes. Besides, a live 
storage capacity of 132 BCM is likely to be created on completion of 
irrigation/multipurpose schemes under various stages of consideration. 
Government of India is also promoting rain water harvesting through 
Watershed Management Programme, artificial recharge of ground water and 
roof-top rain water harvesting under the sector reform project of Accelerated 
Rural Water Supply Programme under the Ministry of Rural Development, 
for which technical and financial a ssistance is provided to the State 
Governments and other implementing agencies. Central Ground Water Board 
has also taken up a Central Sector Scheme on "Studies of Recharge to 
Ground Water" on pilot basis. 
11 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2003] 
As a long term measures, National Water Development Agency have 
formulated National Perspective Plan for water resources development which 
envisages interlinking between various Peninsular rivers and Himalayan 
rivers for transfer of water from surplus basins to water deficit basins which will 
accrue benefits of irrigation, drinking water supply and hydro-power etc.

Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the country's outstanding external debt has shot up from 
$98.76 billion in March 2002 to US$ 104.99 billion in December, 2002; 
(b) if so, whether this will have a serious impact on the Indian economy; 
(c) whether the Government are confident that the country's foreign debt 
position is comfortable and economy is well insulated from possible external 
sector shocks;

†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
66 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) and (b) The external debt stock of the 
country stood at 105.0 billion as at end-December, 2002 against 98.76 billion 
at end-March, 2002. Since important external debt indicators like debt-GDP 
ratio, debt service to current receipts ra tio and short term to total debts ratio 
have progressively shown improvement, a marginal increase in external debt 
is not expected to have any adverse impact on the Indian economy. 
(c) As the external debt indicators have improved substantially over time, 
external debt position of the country is comfortable. 
(d) and (e) No. Sir. The latest Status Report on India's External Debt 
points out that the incidence of external debt burden measured by the debt-GDP 
ratio has declined from 38.7 per cent at end-March, 1992 to 20.6 per cent at 
end-December, 2002, while debts service as per cent to Current Receipts 
declined from 30.2 per cent to 13.7 per cent in the corresponding period. 
Further, the short-term debt as a proporation to foreign exchange assets has 
declined from a high of 382.1 per cent to 5.0 per cent during the same period. 
Cautious and prudent approach towards external debt management pursued 
in 1990 by the Government of India ha s helped to place India in comfortable 
external debt position. The policy focus has been to concentrate on 
concessional and less expensive fund sources, preference for longer maturity 
profile, and enduring vigil on build up of short-term debt, premature 
retirement of high cost external debt and encouragement to non-debt creating 
capital flows.

resources of 1085 BCM.Thus, as per the report, the estimated requirement of 2050

coverage of all habitations by 2004.

providing drinking water facilities to one lakh rural primary 
schools; and revival of one lakh traditional sources of water have 
been approved and an amount of Rs. 700 crore has been 
sanctioned for the purpose. These programmes will be completed 
in 2003-2004 and 2004-2005.

272. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: W ill the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) has identified 
shortage of water as-one of the most worrying problems in the time to come; 
(b) if so, what would be the estimated demand of potable water in India 
during the next five years; 
(c) whether there has been an increase in use of water during the last ten 
years and this demand will increase further during the next decade; and 
(d) if so, what steps Government propose to take to meet the 
requirements of people during the next decade? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) The 
Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) has identified areas showing 
decline in ground water levels. However, no study has been undertaken by 
CGWA for estimation of shortage of ground water in the years to come. 
(c) The population of the country is growing rapidly. As a result, the 
demand of water has also increased a nd the same will increase further during 
next decade. 
(d) In order to augment the availability of water for various uses and their 
efficient use, schemes are planned, investigated, formul ated, implemented 
and funded by the State Governments out of their own resources and as per 
their own priorities. To help the State Governments in their effort, technical and 
financial assistance is provided by the Ministry of Rural Development under 
Accelerated Rural Water Supply programme. Government of India is also 
promoting rain water harvesting through artificial recharge of ground water and 
roof top rain water harvesting. For meeti ng future requirements of water, as a 
long term measure, National Water Development Agency have formulated 
National Perspective Plan for water resources development, which envisages 
inter-linking various Peninsular rivers and Himalayan rivers for transfer of 
water from surplus basin to water deficit basins.

exploitation of ground water?

Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state:

contentious issue among the States in recent times; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the Prime Minister had to intervene to sort 
out the difference between the upper and lower riparian States; 
(c) whether Government are aware of the problems faced by Andhra 
Pradesh due to non-cooperation Karnat aka which is in upper reaches of 
Tunghabhadra and Pannar in times of distress; and 
(d) if so, whether Government have any plan or suggestion to protect the 
interest of lower riparian States like Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) Most of 
the major rivers in India are inter-State in character having catchments/ 
watersheds in two or more States. Often water disputes arise amongest the basin 
States with regard to the use, distribution or control of the waters in respect 
of these inter-state rivers/river valleys or in the interpretation of the terms of 
any agreement relating to the use, distribution or control of such water or in 
the implementation of any such agr eement Actions/steps are undertaken 
through negotiations at all level so that inter-State disputes are resolved for 
optimum development of water resources. 
Under Article 262 of the Constitution, Parliament has enacted Inter-State 
Water Disputes Act, 1956 for adjudication of disputes relating to water of 
Inter-State rivers and river valleys. Acco rding to Section 4 (1) of Inter-State 
Water Disputes Act, 1956, "when any request under Section (3) is received 
from any State Government in respect of any water dispute and the Central 
Government is of the opinion that the water dispute cannot be settled by 
negotiations, the Centra! Government shall, within a period not exceeding one 
year from the data of receipt of such request, by notification in the Official 
Gazette, constitute a Water Dispute Tribunal for the adjudication of the water 
dispute."

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE

conception of unborn child, have come to light in the States of Punjab, 
Haryana, Delhi and Maharashtra. Th e authorities concerned have initiated 
action against the advertisers. The Delhi Government has launched 
prosecution against a weekly magazine 'India Abroad', a monthly magazine 
'Life Positive', and dailies like, Times of India and Punjab Kesari for 
publishing such advertisements in violation of section 22 of the Pre-conception

appropriate action against Malpani Infertility Clinic for issuing advertisement 
on web-site and file compliance report within three weeks.

and spirit and launch prosecution against violators thereof. To strengthen the 
implementation of the Act, regional workshops and training programmes are 
being organised to sensitize the Appropr iate Authorities appointed under the

constituted to monitor the implementation of the Act through field visits. 
Various activities are also being undertaken regularly to create awareness 
through Radio, Television, newspapers, hoardings etc. in various States/UTs. 
Amendments have been made to the Act and Rules with effect from 14.2.2003 
to bring within their ambit the advertisements made on Internet about the 
facilities of pre-natal detection/disclosure of sex of foetus, pre-conception sex 
selection by any means-scientific or otherwise. Other amendments made to the

SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH 'LALAN': 
Will the Minsiter of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that import of a number of Indian goods is still

THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN* 
JAITLEY): (a) One of the fundamental principles of the multilateral trading system 
under WTO is that of the Most Favoured Nation (MFN) Treatment which 
envisages non-discrimination among member countries for the purpose of 
trade.Therefore, discrimination or restrictions specific to India goods by other 
WTO members is not permitted. However, WTO rules authorize restrictions 
on import of goods based on tariff as agreed upon and also through other types 
of restrictions which are permissible. Such permissible restrictions include 
those based on balance of payment grounds, sanitary and phyto sanitary related 
restrictions, conformity with

agreed/international standards and contingent protection measures like anti-
dumping, subsidy and safeguard actions. Procedural requirements could also 
act as barriers to trade. 
Restrictions on import of goods from India exist in several of the WTO 
member countries. When market access is affected in any significant manner 
in specific countries, such issues are taken up, particularly if they are also not 
WTO compatible. Normally such rest rictions on imports are addressed 
through bilateral contacts like inter-governmental commissions, working 
groups on trade and economic cooperation etc. The WTO also provides for a 
number of mechanisms for addressing the issue of restriction on imports of 
goods into the markets by WTO me mbers. These include Trade Policy 
Review Mechanism, discussions in the Councils, subsidiary bodies, bilateral 
consultations and dispute settlement. Such issues are also taken up as part of 
multilateral negotiations.

Tariff reduction formula on access for non-agricultural goods 
*18.SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the World Trade Organisation's (WTO) 
negotiating group on market access for non-agricultural goods has included a 
tariff reduction formula suggested by India in its revised note on formula 
approaches; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) in what way India's tariff reducti on formula is different from the 
earlier one? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN 
JAITLEY): (a) to (c) Indi a's specific tariff reduction proposal submitted on 
30 December 2002 vide Document No. TN/MA/W/10 Add. 1 was reflected in 
the WTO Secretariat's compilation of the proposals submitted on tariff reduction 
modalities by Members to the Negotiating Group on Market Access for non-
agricultural goods. However, it was not included in the Annex listing the formula 
reduction methods submitted by Members. 
India refined its specific proposal by presenting it in a mathematical form 
with quantification of the flexibilities sought and submitted the same to the 
WTO on 14 March 2003 vide Document No. TN/MA/W/10 Add. 2. This 
revised submission was subsequently included in the Annex listing the formula 
methodologies in the revision of the WTO Secretariat's compilation presented 
to Members on 1 April 2003 vide Document No. TN/MA/6 Rev. 1 
It may also be mentioned that on 16 May 2003 the Chairman of the 
Negotiating Group on Market Access submitted on his own responsibility a set 
of draft modalities for Members consid eration. These.drafts, circulated vide 
Doucment No.TN/MAAA//35 is presently being discussed. 
158 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
India's tariff reduction proposal inter-alia required a simple percentage cut on 
bound tariffs of each Member, with a higher percentage to be set for developed 
countries than the percentage set for developing countries. Additionally, Members 
were required not to impose tariff on any product in excess of three times their 
average tariff. The average for this purpose was to be calculated after effecting 
the tariff reduction. 
While India did not specify what the reduction percentage would be for 
developed and developi ng countries, as an illu stration the reduction on 
different tariff lines using a 50-33.33% and 45-30% ratio was included in the 
paper. 
For unbound tariff lines, it was proposed that developing countries could 
bind them at the highest of the bound rates in a Member's tariff schedule or at 
the applied rate on a cut off date whichever was higher. 
Integral to the Indian proposal were also two provisions as special and 
differential measures for developing coun tries. These were (a) flexibility to 
decide individual tariff bindings on at least 15% of the bound tariff lines, on 
the understanding that the overall percentage reduction will be achieved; and 
(b) at least up to 10% of the presently unbound tariff lines considered sensitive 
or strategically important for a developing country could continue to be left 
unbound.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI SATYABRATA M OOKHERJEE); (a) and (b)The 
agenda for the Fifth Session of the Ministerial Conference of the WTO, 
scheduled to be held in Cancun (Mexico) during 10-14 September 2003, has not

Doha, as contained the Doha Ministeria l Declaration the Fifth Session of the

184 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
consistently taken the stand during these negotiations that the development 
dimension of the Work Programme should be maintained and should not be 
diluted at any cost. 
Agriculture sector provides livelihood for the large majority of the 
people in India and negotiations in agriculture should result in tangible 
improvement in the living conditions of low-income and resource poor 
farmers and landless agricultural labourers. This cannot be achieved unless 
there is significant and meaningful reduction in domestic support and all forms 
of export subsidies in major developed countries. Further more, concerns 
relating to food security and livelihood of farmers should be addressed through 
effective protection at the border for their produce and sufficient flexibility to 
apply safeguards to address different situations. 
In respect of non-agricultural pro ducts, India has strongly advocated 
increased market access for products of  export interest to India including 
products such as textiles and leather goods. India has also stressed the need 
for providing for 'less than full reciprocity' in the matter of reduction 
commitments by developing countries. Expressing positive interest in the 
services' negotiations, India has asked for greater and effective liberalization 
in the movement of natural persons under Mode 4. 
On the so-called Singapore issues, namely Trade and Investment; Trade 
and Competition Policy; Transparency in Government Procurement; and Trade 
Facilitation, views of the Members of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) 
are still divergent on many of the key aspects being discussed. Greater clarity 
would be required before any decision on modalities could be considered. 
India has been taking steps at bilateral, plurilateral and multilateral levels, 
both with developed and developing country partners, aimed at resolution of 
issues of particular interest to developing countries such as TRIPS and Public 
Health; Special and Differential Treatment; and Implementation-related 
issues, on a priority basis so as to have a successful outcome at the Cancun 
Ministerial Conference.

23. SHRI MURLI DEORA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state:

(d) whether crediting of export remittances by Banks in exporters' 
account is delayed;

competitiveness of the Indian exporters in the global market as compared to

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) The existing 
interest rate structure of export credit in  rupees as well as in foreign currency 
is: 
In Rupees: 
Not exceeding Prime Lending Rate (PLR) minus 2.5 percentage points 
for pre-shipment credit upto 180 da ys, against incentives receivable 
from Government covered by ECGC guarantee upto 90 days and for 
post-shipment credit (demand bills for transit period as specified by 
FEDAI, usance bills, undrawn balances and retention money for 
supply portion only) upto 90 days. 
Banks are free to decide the rate of interest to be charged, keeping in view 
the PLR and the spread guidelines, for pre-shipment credit beyond 180 
days and upto 270 days, post-shipment credit beyond 90 days and upto 6 
months from the date of shipment, deferred credit for periods beyond 
180 days and for pre-shipment and post-shipment export credit not 
otherwise specified. 
In Foreign Currency: 
Not exceeding 0.75% over LIBO R/EUROLIBOR/EURIBOR for pre-
shipment credit upto 180 days, on demand bills for transit 
186 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
period as specified by FEDAI, usance bills upto six months from the 
date of shipment. Interest rate applicable for above mentioned period 
plus 2.0 percentage points for pre-shipment credit beyond 180 days and 
upto 360 days and for both demand and usance export bills on post-
shipment credit basis. 
Banks are free to decide the rate of interest, keeping in view the PLR 
and the spread guidelines, for export credit not otherwise specified on 
both pre and post shipment credit basis. 
China provides suppliers credit for Chinese exporters for which the rate is 
decided by the Central Bank, i.e. the People's Bank of China. In the case of 
Exim Bank of China, it is not bound by the OECD Consensus and interest 
support is offered by the National Department of Finance. Reports indicate 
that in the case of China effective export credit interest rates are often lower 
than the Commercial Interest Reference Rates (CIRR). Exim Bank of China is 
the policy bank of China and its business is completely underwritten by the 
Government of China. 
(b) and (c) Exim Bank through a study conducted on "Transaction Cost 
of India Exports" has observed that transaction costs of Indian exports have 
declined in recent years. In case of textiles, the transaction costs have declined 
from 15% in 1998 to 3-10% of export revenue. Significant declines have also 
been observed in the case of engineering goods, chemicals, computer software 
and agro industries. In case of pha rmaceuticals, the decline is modest 
compared to other sectors. Transacti on costs are perceived to be of the 
magnitude of 5-10% of export revenue in case of electronics and electrical 
machinery, paper products and plastic components. 
(d) RBI has advised Banks to promptly pass on credit to the customers 
on realisation of export bills. Banks have also been instructed to pay 
compensation stipulated by FEDAI to the exporter client, in case of delay in 
affording credit to the exporters; account in respect of payment advices received, 
complete in all respects, without waiting for a demand from the exporter. Banks 
have-also been advised to devise a sy stem to monitor timely credit of the

Known as DOTS, which is a WHO recommended strategy, is being

60. SHRI MURLIDEORA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether scientists at Bhabha At omic Research Centre measured 
polonium-210 levels in tobacco which is an alpha particles emitting 
radioactive element; 
(b) whether radioactivity in cigarette acco unts for at least 90 per cent of 
all smoking related cancers; 
(c) whether PO-210 float in the ambient air for the passive neighbours to 
inhale; and 
(d) whether in view of the above, Government proposed to have a 
complete ban on cigarette smoking in the interest of health of the citizens and if 
not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) Yes. Sir. 
(b) According to the Bhabha Research Centre, direct correlation between 
radioactivity in cigarettes and smoking related concerns has not yet been 
established. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) In order to tackle the adve rse effects of tobacco use, a 
comprehensive legislation, namely The Cigarettes and other Tobacco 
Products (Prohibition of Advertisement and Regulation of Trade and 
Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 2003" has been 
enacted by the Parliament recently. The Act intends to discourage the 
use of tobacco products through various control measures like total 
ban on advertisement of tobacco products, prohibition of smoking in 
public places and ban on sale of to bacco products to persons below 
18 years of age and within a radius of 100 yards of educational 
institutions.

FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) There Is a proposal to introduce a

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) No Sir. The position is that

report, instances of serious lapses on the part of the Government Hospitals 
and private nursing homes in the matter of management of biomedical 
wastes;

Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & 
Technology, Environment and Forests on Demands for Grants (2003-04) of 
the Ministry of Environment & Forests has, inter-alia observed that the 
scientific management of medical wastes is dangerously neglected in the 
country. The staff charged with the responsibility for sanitation, cleanliness in

video piracy like a recommendation by the Committee for 
development of the entertainment sector set up to suggest the policy 
framework both at the Centre and in the States, to fix a ceiling for 
entertainment tax at 60%, organization of training courses and 
removal of excise duty on CDs.

• The best cinema in any year is selected as part of the 'Indian 
Panorama'. These films are especially shown to audiences on the 
festival circuit in order to create, as well as cater to, a taste for Indian 
cinema.

Television Institutes, Kolkata and Pune.

makers.

of India to promote cinema.

State Governments offer incentives to their local film industry in the nature of 
subsidies, loans of entertainment tax exemptions.

90. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) the guidelines for granting the Direct-To-Home licence to the 
Electronic Media TV; 
(b) whether the guidelines have been followed in all the cases before 
granting letter of intent during the last one year; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING (SHRI RAVI S HANKAR PRASAD): (a) Detailed 
guidelines for starting DTH service we re issued in March, 2001. The 
guidelines, inter alia, provide that:— 
• The licensee company shall be an Indian company, registered under 
the Indian Companies Act, 1956; 
• Licensee shall adhere to programme and advertisement codes 
256 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
laid down by Ministry of Information and Broadcasting from time to 
time; 
• All foreign personnel likely to be deployed by way of appointment, 
contract, consultancy etc. by the licensee for installation, maintenance 
and operation of the licencee's serv ice shall be required to obtain 
security clearance from the Government of India prior to their 
deployment; 
• All content provided by the DTH platform to the subscribers, 
irrespective of its source, shall pass through the encryption and 
conditional access system, located within the earth station situated on 
Indian soil; 
• The licensee shall ensure that its facilities are not used for 
transmission of any objectionable or obscene content, messages or 
communication inconsistent with the laws of India; 
• The licensee shall provide the necessary facility for continuous 
monitoring of the DTH broadcasting service at its own cost and 
maintain the recordings of programmes and advertisements carried on 
the platform for a period of ninety days from the date of broadcast and 
produce the same to the licensor or its authorized representative, as and 
when required; 
• The licensee will, if required by the licensor or its authorized 
representative, provide necessary facilities for continuous monitoring 
for any particular aspect of the licensee's activities and operations; 
• the applicant is required to fulfil the eligibility criteria laid down in the 
DTH guidelines and is also subject to security and technical clearances 
from the concerned departments. 
The guidelines are available on this Ministry's website: mib.nic.in. 
(b) No 'letter of intent' has been issued so far to any of the applicant 
companies. Guidelines are strictly followed while processing the applications 
for DTH licence.

cultural ethos of India? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING (SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): (a) and (b) 
The Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) certifies films under the 
provisions of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 and the guidelines issued 
thereunder. The objectives of film certification are to ensure that: 
(i) the medium of film remains responsible and sensitive to the values and 
standards of society; 
(ii)  artistic expression and creative freedom are not unduly curbed; 
(iii)  certification is responsive to social change; 
(iv) the medium of film provides clean and health entertainment; and 
(v) as far as possible, the film is of aesthetic value and cinematically of a 
good standard. 
The following guidelines in the Cinematograph (Certification) Rules, 1991 
address the concerns raised: 
2(vii) Human sensibilities are not offended by vulgarity, obscenity or 
depravity;

2(x) Scenes involving sexual violence against women like attempt to rape,

and if any such incident is germane to the theme, they shall be reduced 
to the minimum and not details are shown; 
2(xi) Scenes showing sexual perversion shall be avoided and if such matters 
are germane to the theme, they sh all be reduced to the minimum and 
no details are shown.

Entry of old vessels in ports 
108. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of SHIPPING be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Paris MOU, an organisation of 20 IMO 
member countries, that monitors international standards has stipulated 
275 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2003] 
that certain categories of old vessels would be disallowed from entering its 
member ports without permission and inspection of its safety standards; 
(b) whether 36.5 per cent of our vessels which are 20 years old and 42.5 
per cent which are 10 years old would be affected; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SHIPPING (SHRI 
DILIP KUMAR MANSUKHLAL GANDHI):(a) Yes Sir. Paris MOU, a 
regional organization of 20 IMO member countries mainly from the European 
Region established to co-ordinate Po rt State Control inspections in the 
Region, is going to introduce some new requirements with effect from 22nd 
July, 2003 on all the vessels entering ports of its member countries. Under the 
new requirements, some of the vessels may be refused access on the basis of 
number of detentions under Port State Control in the Paris MOU region in the 
previous 2 years. 
(b) and (c) There is no separate category proposed to be created under the 
new requirements between vessels of 10 years age and vessels of 20 years age 
and over. Categorization of the vessels under the new requirements which 
will be subjected to mandatory expanded inspection every 12 months is on the 
following lines : 
• Oil tankers over 3000 GRT and over 15 years old. 
• Chemical and Gas carriers over 10 years old. 
• Bulk carriers over 12 years old. 
• Passenger ships over 15 years old. 
In addition, new stipulation relates to inspection of ship on the basis of 
target factor which includes elements like previous inspection records of the 
ship, flag states rating based on performance of its ship under Paris MOU, 
classification status, type and age of the vessels. Any vessel, which has a 
target factor of 50 or more will be subjected to monthly inspections, if it calls 
Paris MOU member countries ports. Since the criteria as stated above are not 
based on age of the vessels being 
276 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
over 20 years and 10 years, the projected percentage figures are not apply. 
However, considering the Port State Control detention details of Indian ships 
since January 2002 under Paris MOU, no Indian ship comes in the above 
categories i.e. the ships which can be refused access or will be required to be 
inspected every month. In so far as expanded inspection requirements are 
concerned, Indian tankers, passenger sh ips, chemical and gas carriers do not 
generally operate in Paris MOU region . Therefore the new requirements of 
expanded inspections will affect only the Indian bulk carriers of over 12 years 
in age and most of Indian bulk carrier s are in this age group. However, under 
the Safety Convention requirements all the ships are required to be in full 
readiness always to undergo expanded inspections successfully.

.     125.      SHRI N.R. DASARI: 
SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN: 
Will the Minister of URB AN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that  Municipalities in the small and 
medium towns are facing fiscal stress b ecause of their inability of increase 
upon their principal sources of revenue; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the remedial measures proposed to be taken 
by Government to improve the functioning of the municipalities in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI PON 
RADHAKRISHNAN): (a) and (b) Municipalities, particularly in small and 
medium towns were facing fiscal difficulties due to their limited financial 
298 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
resources as well as limited access to generate revenue. A provision was, 
therefore made in the Constitution (74th Amendment) Act, 1992 itself for 
constitution of Finance Commissions at the State level in every five years to 
review the financial position of the municipalities and make recommendations 
to the State Government with regard to taxation; sharing of taxes between the 
State Government and Local Government; principles for governing grant-in-
aid; and measures for improving the financial position of urban local bodies. 
Suitable amendment has also been made to Article 280 of the Constitution to 
make it mandatory that the Central Finance Commission shall, inter-alia, 
make specific recommendations with regard to measures that are needed to 
augment the resources of a State with a view to supplementing the resources 
of municipalities in the State Fina nce Commission. This amendment has 
helped setting up of a proper linkage among local bodies, State Government 
and the Central Government. 
The State Governments have amended their Municipal Laws to devolve 
adequate functional and financial powers to municipalities in conformity 
with the provisions enshirned in the Constitution (74th Amendment) Act. 
However, as per Entry 5 of the State List of the Constitution, 
'municipality' is a State Subject. In view of this, it is for the State 
Governments to take necessary steps in augmenting financial resources of the 
municipalities and assisting them to come out of the fiscal stress, thereby 
improving their functioning. Nevertheless, the Government of India have 
initiated a number of schemes/programmes to bring in fresh breeze of reforms 
in the urban sector. These include: 
• Setting up of Urban Reforms Incentive Fund to provide reform-linked 
assistance to States with an initial allocation of Rs. 500 crores in the 
Union Budget 2002-03; 
• State-level Pooled Financing Structure to facilitate small and medium 
size urban local bodies to access capital market for investment in 
essential municipal infrastructure, development or bankable urban 
infrastructure projects and introduction of necessary reforms (e.g. tariff 
& financial) in the urban local bodies; 
• Tax-free Municipal Bonds for issue by urban local bodies for 
299 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2003] 
potable water supply, sewerage or sanitation, drainage, solid waste 
management, roads/bridges/flyovers, and urban transport. In addition, 
the Central Government has announced tax exemption in case of bonds 
issued by municipal/local Governments for raising resources for urban 
infrastructure. 
• Setting up of a City Challenge Fund for catalysing city level 
economic reform programmes. 
• Public-Private Participation Guidelines are prepared for providing 
directions to States and municipalities to manage the process of 
involving the private sector in infrastructure development. 
• The Minsitry issued Property Tax Guidelines in 1988 to all State 
Governments with the objective of simplification and rationalization 
of property tax, which is considered as one of the best source of 
revenue for the urban local bodies. States like Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, 
Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka are in the process of 
implementing property tax reforms.

the metropolitan cities particularly of Hyderabad and NCT Delhi on daily and 
monthly basis; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what efforts Government have made  to meet the requirements of 
these cities and to maintain the water quality supplied to the dwellers of these 
metropolitan cities? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI PON 
RADHAKRISHNAN): (a) to (c) Urban water supply being a State subject, it is 
the responsibility of the respective State Governments/Urban Local Bodies to 
plan, formulate, execute, operate and maintain water supply facilities in their 
respective areas and to make adequate provision in their respective State 
Plans. The Government of India supplements the efforts of the State 
Governments through policy formulati on, technical guidance, etc. for 
provision of drinking water facilities. There is also a Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme of Accelerated Urba n Water Supply Programme (AUWSP) since 
1993-94 for providing water supply facilities in smaller towns having population 
less than 20,000 as per 1991 census under which funds are provided by Centre 
and States on 50:50 basis. 
The responsibility for assessment of water requirements for future needs 
rests with the Agencies of the State Governments and local bodies. The projected 
drinking water demand for Hyderabad city as assessed by the Hyderabad 
Metropolitan Water Supply & Sewerage Board for the years 2004, 2016 and 
2021 are 245 MGD, 360 MGD and 400 MGD, respectively. 
Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board has 
informed that Krishna Drinking Water Supply Project for bringing additional 
treated water to Hyderabad metropolitan area from Nagarjunasagar has been 
taken up. 
The Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi has assessed 
302 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
Water requirement for Delhi as 828 MGD against which Delhi Jal Board has an 
installed capacity of about 650 MGD. But the Board is producing 670 MGD of 
Water on an average by optimization. 
As regards National Capital Territory of Delhi, the measures taken by 
Delhi Jal Board to meet the water requirement are given in the Statement 
{See below). 
As regards maintaining of quality of water supplied to the dweller, the 
State Agencies/concerned urban local bodies are required to collect samples of 
raw water periodically at intake points, treated water after each unit operation 
at treatment plant, clear water reservoirs at strategic points in the tranmission 
and distribution system and also at consumers' end for analysis. 
Delhi Jal Board have informed that about 300 water samples are lifted 
daily and tested by well equipped laborato ries. It has also been stated that 
water quality conforms to the standards laid down by CPHEEO. 
Delhi Jal Board have further informed that about 1000 samples are 
checked for presence of residual chlori ne by the Field Engineers. Wherever 
any deficiency is noticed, immediate remedial action is taken and supply of 
potable water through tankers is given during the rectification period.

MATTER RAISED WITH PERMISSION 
Withdrawal of Charges by CBI against highly placed accused 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Sir, what about the 
motion which we had given to you to raise a discussion under rule 170? 
Notice has been given under rule 168, and the discussion should take place 
under 170. I have pointed out in the motion that we would not like to interfere 
with the functioning of the Judiciary or any sub judice matter, but, surely, 
from the precedents which have been followed on earlier occasions, 
330 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
there is a scope that even if a motion appears, partly, to be sub judice, the part 
which is not sub judice can be discussed, and it has been discussed in the past. 
Once it was discussed in a motion moved by Shri N.G. Ranga on 7 th April, 
1966, and, again, in another motion on 16 th of November, 1971. It was 
discussed; though the motion appeared to be sub judice, the Speaker gave a 
ruling that if the entire matter was not sub judice, a part of it could be 
discussed. I have given a motion for discussion and I am reading that motion : 
"This House is of the opinion that the partisan manner in which CBI is 
utilized to abuse the legal process, to subvert the rule of law in the Babri 
Masjid Demolition case, is highly condem nable." This issue is agitating the 
mind of the people due to which we could not transact the normal business in 
the Question Hour today morning. A similar thing happened in the other 
House also, but I am not making any re ference to that. What we said on the 
floor of this House is that we re quire a satisfactor y response from the 
Government on various issues which have arisen in connection with the 
withdrawal of the charge -sheet where certain persons were accused of 
hatching a conspiracy under IPC 120 (B). It was not in the original FIR which 
was brought, but, subsequently, in the course of investigations, over a long 
period of time, another FIR was filed. Thereafter, the CBI submitted a 
consolidated FIR which was taken note of, taken cognisance of, by the Court. 
In course of time, certain legal infirmities came up. The higher Judiciary 
directed the Executive to rectify those, but nothing has happened. In between, 
just two weeks before, we were confronted with a situation that the status quo 
ante, prevailing in the first FIR almost ten years ago, has been restored. And 
whatever investigation has been done by the CBI in this case -- and the CBI 
was working under the direct control of  the Chief of the Union Executive, 
that is, the Prime Minister -- they ha ve simply withdrawn the cases against 
some of the very highly placed accused. To our assessment of the situation, 
this is not only a misuse of the CBI as an investigating agency, but is also 
subverting the rule of law by influencing the judicial process which is on. We 
have no intention to influence the decision of the court in either way. It is for 
the court to decide on the basis of the merits of the witnesses on the evidences 
which are being produced, but the investigating agency which is working 
directly under the Government of India, of which the Prime Minister is 
responsible, if they do certain things  which are not properly appreciated by 
the wider public opinion of this country, then, definitely, Parliament should 
have the right to discuss it and to arrive at its own conclusion. Keeping that 
objective in view, we have tabled this Motion.   And, most respectfully, Sir, I 
331 

RAJYA SABHA [22 July, 2003] 
would like to submit to you to kindly allow this Motion to be debated. Let the 
House express its opinion. Let the legal aspects and political aspects be 
debated and discussed without having any interference with the due process 
of law, without having any reflection in  the course of trial which will take 
place independently in the respective c ourts. Parliament has nothing to do 
with it, but, surely, Parliament has ever y right to express its opinion when the 
premier investigating agency of the country is being misued or is being 
abused to subvert the due process of law. With these observations, Sir, I 
submit it for your consideration. 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU (W est Bengal): Sir, I will just briefly add 
to what Mr. Mukherjee ha s said as all of us, across the Opposition, have 
jointly signed the notice which we have served. Now, Sir, in the very 
beginning of the assumption of office by this Government, we had expressed 
our apprehension that we are going towards a situation where- so far as the 
Babri Masjid demolition case is concer ned-- the accused and the prosecution 
are one and the same. And, there was a clear-cut conflict of interest. 
Therefore, at any given point in time,  there may arise a situation where we 
will find that the prosecution has been sabotaged and the entire judicial 
process has been subverted and undermined, and it is precisely that is what 
has happened. The original investigation which was undertaken by the CID 
which was found inadequate, which was expanded. And, the CBI submitted 
the expanded chargesheet. Now, we see a particular provision of law being 
dropped from that chargesheet and the evidence that was collected by the CBI 
being dropped by the Government in the latest chargesheet which is being 
submitted. Therefore, Sir, in the fitness of things, it is our case that the 
conduct of the prosecution is very much  an issue in which the Executive is 
involved and Parliament is well within its right to discuss that issue and give 
its opinion. 
Sir, we will just give a parallel example. Last year, after the Godhra 
incident, when, in Gujarat, communal clashes and communal attacks took 
place against minorities, the National Human Rights Commission had given a 
suggestion that some of the major cases including the Godhra incident itself 
and four other major cases including the Best Bakery case should be tried by 
the CBI. I distinctly remember that the hon. Law Minister -- he is also here 
today - mentioned, "that will sabotage the prosecution because the 
investigation and prosecution by the ag encies there are at a very advanced 
stage, in all these cases. Therefore, if  we now go to CBI, that will sabotage 
and undermine the prosecution."     Now, we have 
332 

[22 July, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
seen, a few days back, what has happ ened to the effectiveness of the
